common_name: Neches White Clover (Early-Flowering Texas A&M White Clover)

planting.note: Sow in fall or late winter; Neches, released by Texas A&M AgriLife Research at Overton, flowers earlier than Durana and carries noticeably larger leaves, giving it a fast start as a nitrogen-fixing groundcover in Gulf South pastures and orchard alleys.

directions: Broadcast inoculated seed onto a firm, weed-free seedbed in fall and rake lightly to press it into good contact with the soil. Neches was bred at the Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center in Overton from a synthetic cross of pest-resistant USDA breeding lines and East Texas ecotypes, and it reaches full bloom noticeably earlier in spring than older intermediate white clovers, with leaves roughly a fifth larger than Durana. Its early flowering makes it a strong nectar source for pollinators before summer heat arrives, while its creeping stolons knit together a dense, low mat that suppresses winter weeds and fixes nitrogen for a following warm-season planting. Mow occasionally to keep the stand vigorous and prevent taller companion grasses or weeds from shading it out.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center, Overton

common_name: Louisiana S-1 White Clover (Heat- and Drought-Tolerant Gulf South White Clover)

planting.note: Sow in fall for overwintering cover, or late winter in mild Gulf Coast climates; Louisiana S-1 was selected by the LSU AgCenter specifically for better heat and drought tolerance than common ladino white clover strains.

directions: Broadcast inoculated seed onto a firm, prepared bed in fall and rake lightly so the small seed makes good soil contact. Louisiana S-1 is an intermediate-type white clover developed by the LSU AgCenter to outlast common ladino clover through the long, humid summers and periodic drought typical of the Gulf South, while still flowering steadily through the growing season to support pollinators. It spreads readily by stolons to form a dense living mulch beneath fruit trees, in orchard rows, or overseeded into warm-season pasture grasses, fixing nitrogen that benefits neighboring plantings. Where summers turn hot and dry it reliably persists and reseeds better than northern-bred white clover cultivars, making it a dependable long-term groundcover rather than a one-season planting.

common_name: RegalGraze Ladino Clover (Grazing-Tolerant Giant White Clover)

planting.note: Sow in fall or late winter; RegalGraze is a large-leaved ladino-type white clover bred for heavier grazing and mowing tolerance than older ladino strains, tested favorably against them by the University of Georgia.

directions: Broadcast inoculated seed onto a firm, prepared seedbed in fall or late winter and rake lightly, since the tiny seed needs shallow, even coverage to establish well. RegalGraze is a giant ladino-type white clover with an upright habit, fine stems, and unusually large dark-green leaves that regrow vigorously after close mowing or heavy grazing, a trait bred into the cultivar to outperform older ladino types under repeated defoliation in University of Georgia trials. It lacks the cyanogenic compounds found in some small- and intermediate-leaved white clovers, making it a safer forage choice where that matters. Interseed it into dormant warm-season pasture grasses in fall for a nitrogen-fixing winter forage, or let it run as a dense flowering groundcover in orchard alleys where regular mowing is planned.

common_name: Talladega Crimson Clover (Late-Maturing Reseeding Crimson Clover)

planting.note: Sow in fall for a winter-to-spring cover crop; Talladega matures roughly a week later than Dixie, Auburn, and Autauga crimson clover, extending the bloom and reseeding window into late spring.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a prepared seedbed in fall, raking lightly for good seed-to-soil contact. Talladega is one of the later-maturing named reseeding crimson clover cultivars, flowering roughly a week after earlier types like Dixie and Auburn, which spreads out the bloom period when it is grown alongside an earlier cultivar in a blend. Its hard-seeded nature gives it strong volunteer reseeding from year to year once a stand is established and allowed to flower and drop seed at least once. Terminate by mowing or rolling at early flower for maximum nitrogen contribution ahead of a spring crop, or let a portion of the stand go to seed each year to maintain a self-sustaining crimson clover planting.
sources: Auburn University Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Amclo Arrowleaf Clover (Early-Maturing Dark-Seeded Arrowleaf Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill in fall on well-drained soil; Amclo is an early-maturing arrowleaf clover cultivar, one of the original dark-seeded selections alongside Yuchi and Meechee that founded the modern arrowleaf breeding lines.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a well-prepared, well-drained bed in early fall and lightly cover, since arrowleaf clover establishes slowly at first but grows rapidly once cool weather sets in. Amclo is an early-maturing arrowleaf clover cultivar with dark, hard seed, developed as part of the same breeding work that produced Yuchi and Meechee, and its earlier flowering makes it a useful choice for pairing with later cultivars to extend bloom and nitrogen-fixing coverage across the spring. Its tall, upright stems topped with pinkish-white flower heads distinguish it in a mixed planting from lower-growing clovers, and it reseeds well on well-drained upland soils when allowed to flower before termination. Mow or graze before the plants become too woody and fibrous, since arrowleaf clover forage quality declines as it approaches full maturity.
sources: Auburn University Alabama Agricultural Experiment Station
Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center, Overton

common_name: Blackhawk Arrowleaf Clover (Disease-Resistant Texas A&M Arrowleaf Clover)

planting.note: Broadcast or drill in fall on well-drained soil; Blackhawk, released by Texas A&M AgriLife Research at Overton, was bred for improved resistance to Pythium seedling disease and bean yellow mosaic virus compared with older arrowleaf cultivars.

directions: Broadcast seed onto a well-prepared, well-drained bed in early fall and lightly cover, since arrowleaf clover germinates slowly at first but grows quickly once cool, moist conditions arrive. Blackhawk was developed at the Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center in Overton through recurrent selection from Yuchi, Amclo, and Meechee breeding lines for tolerance to Pythium seedling blight and bean yellow mosaic virus, two problems that had eroded stand reliability in older arrowleaf cultivars by the late twentieth century. Its seed coat is almost entirely black, a useful field identifier, and it matures slightly earlier than the older Apache cultivar while offering broader multi-disease tolerance. Because arrowleaf clover requires well-drained soil and does poorly in wet, poorly drained fields, reserve it for upland plantings rather than low, seasonally wet ground.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Research and Extension Center, Overton

planting.note: Broadcast onto a firm seedbed in fall; Woogenellup is one of the most widely grown subterranean clover cultivars in the southeastern Coastal Plain, adapted from southern Texas to Florida and comparatively tolerant of iron-deficiency chlorosis.

directions: Broadcast seed over a firm, moist bed in early fall and rake lightly, since good seed-to-soil contact is essential for even establishment. Woogenellup is a widely planted Australian-bred subterranean clover cultivar that has proven well adapted to the southeastern Coastal Plain from southern Texas through Florida, and it shows comparatively good tolerance of iron-deficiency chlorosis relative to many other subterranean clover cultivars, though it can still show symptoms on high-pH calcareous soils. Like other subterranean clovers, it buries its own seed pods just below the soil surface after flowering, which lets a stand reseed itself reliably without replanting in most years. Its dense, low, mat-forming growth makes an excellent living mulch and winter weed suppressor under fruit trees or in orchard alleys, dying back naturally as temperatures rise in late spring.

common_name: Villana Hairy Vetch (Low-Volunteer-Seed Grazing and Cover Crop Vetch)

planting.note: Sow in fall for a winter-to-spring cover crop or forage; Villana hairy vetch produces less hard, volunteer-prone seed than many common hairy vetch strains, reducing its tendency to become a weed in the following crop.

directions: Broadcast or drill inoculated seed into a prepared seedbed in fall, ideally with a companion cereal grain such as rye or wheat to give the vining growth something to scramble up. Villana hairy vetch was selected to carry a lower hard-seed count than many older hairy vetch strains, which means less seed persists in the soil to sprout as a volunteer weed in the crop that follows, an advantage for growers who want the nitrogen-fixing benefits of hairy vetch without the reseeding headache. It forms a dense, sprawling winter mat that suppresses weeds effectively and provides good-quality grazing or hay in addition to its cover crop role. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or grazing at or shortly after flowering to capture peak biomass and nitrogen contribution ahead of a spring planting.
